INSPIRATION FOR 
PROGRAMME 


YOUR NATURE 

by P. M. Taschereau, Naturalist, 
Woodland Boys 3 Camp, Quebec 
Nova Scotia Museum of Science. 


Adapted from a talk given by the author at the Nova Scotia Camping Association Camp 
Directors’ Seminar, 1963. 


Have you ever considered what it is 
you do for a child when you give him 
an interest in natural history? I have 
found that you can give him an interest 
so all-engrossing that he will never be 
without something to do; that you can 
stimulate a lifetime hobby or avocation. 
Nature study is a physical activity that 
takes one out-of-doors in the woods, 
fields, fresh air and sunlight. It gives 
a familiarity with native plants and 
animals that immeasurably increases 
one’s enjoyment of the out-of-doors. 
Hiking becomes more enjoyable and 
interesting when one recognizes familiar 
objects along the trail. Its discipline 
increases manual dexterity. (The student 
of insects soon learns the delicate care 
required in observing and handling 
such creatures.) 

Nature study is an intellectual 
activity. By encouraging observation it 
sharpens the senses and increases one’s 
awareness of the beauty and immense 
diversity of the life around us. Wonder 
is the pathway to knowledge; it stimu¬ 
lates the desire for knowledge that 
leads to understanding. And while 
there is a pleasure in seeing something 
beautiful, there is a far greater joy in 
understanding it as well. 

Nature study for camps is not bi¬ 
ology, nor is it science though it may 
be scientific. Nature study at camp is 
designed to encourage the interest of 
children and open their eyes to things 
really worth knowing in the world 


about them. It begins with what is at 
hand and of immediate interest, and 
its goal is the heightening and deepen¬ 
ing of that wonder and ‘desire to know’ 
inherent in every human being. Cam¬ 
pers must first experience the adventure 
of exploring, the excitement of dis¬ 
covery and the fun of collecting before 
they are ready for more serious pur¬ 
suits in this area. 

Methods of Camp Nature Study 

The nature programme must be cor¬ 
related to the total camp programme, 
making use of opportunities as they 
come along. It is centered around the 
camp museum and consists of hikes, 
talks, activities and stories, much of 
the instruction being prompted by the 
spontaneous enquiry of the campers 
themselves. 

A small library and a space set aside 
for specimens is the first step in bring¬ 
ing natural history into the camp pro¬ 
gramme. If there is no camp naturalist, 
one of the counsellors who has an 
interest in nature can supervise, and 
with the help of senior campers, label 
some of the specimens brought in and 
look up answers to questions. Care must 
be taken lest the collections become, 
dusty, meaningless accumulations of 
junk. They should be labelled, clean, 
orderly and meaningful. 

Point out things of interest as they 
are discovered. Clam trails seen at 
morning dip, mosquito larvae in the 


48 


Canadian Camping 



rain barrel, a dragonfly emerging from 
its nymphal skin, the camouflage of 
birds—they are all worth calling to 
the campers’ attention. There are 
nature games suitable for the whole 
camp, and a nature story forms a most 
suitable closing for the campfire. 

Many instances can be taken advan¬ 
tage of in working nature into the pro¬ 
gramme. On the first day of camp 
the naturalist is called upon to outline 
the boundaries, describe the waterfront, 
tell something of the camp’s history 
and some of the wild life the campers 
may expect to see. This might be 
followed up by a hike around the 
property during which places of interest 
—or poison ivy to be avoided—could 
be pointed out. 

Attempts made to ‘landscape’ tents 
or cabins by transplanting young trees 
or shrubs or other wild material can be 
rewarded by extra points at inspection. 
Art work done on a bracket fungus 
can be very attractive as well as in¬ 
structive. What is a bracket fungus? 
Where are you most likely to find one? 
A fungus hunt could be organized and 
a competition held for the largest 
bracket fungus found, concluding with 
an exhibit and judging of the art work. 
At a boys’ camp one noon hour the 
head table was seen to be adorned 
with an artistic display of ferns, mosses, 
and clubmosses planted in an old tin 
plate covered with shiny new tinfoil. 
This initiated a table beautifying con¬ 
test—at the next meal each table had 
centre-pieces of small green plants. 

Nature can be worked into the crafts 
period by the use of natural materials. 
Basswood whistles are popular and 
pieces of driftwood or beaver-chewed 
wood can be made into attractive lamp 
bases. The natural bend in the tap 
root of many young trees can become 
the handle of a staff. The identification 
of the various kinds of hard and soft 
woods used in fire-building, and the 


situations in which these are found, can 
make a good campcraft topic. 

Bulletin Boards 

Apart from the board at the museum, 
a general nature bulletin board may be 
placed near or in the dining hall where 
it will catch the attention of campers. 
Lists of birds, trees, and other observa¬ 
tions are posted here. Pictures of 
poison ivy, or the plant itself behind a 
plastic sheet, along with clippings of 
interest taken from newspapers and 
magazines are pinned on the board. A 
group of interested campers may be 
appointed as curators and the an¬ 
nouncements changed frequently to 
maintain interest. Things of interest at 
the museum can be advertised, and a 
shelf may be placed below the bulletin 
board to hold a specimen or a con¬ 
tainer of water for a small plant. 

Answering Questions 

“What is it?” or “What’s this 
called?” will become familiar questions 
to anyone who takes on the job of 
nature leader, as will the reply “I don’t 
know” to which should be added “Let’s 
see if we can find out.” 

This “let’s learn together” attitude 
should be the approach for any leader 
not a specialist in his subject. Indeed, 
the more learned and competent a 
specialist is, the more readily does he 
admit his ignorance when he doesn’t 
know, or is uncertain of, the answer 
to a question. As Herb Groh has writ¬ 
ten, “The mark of a leader is not as 
one young genius put it, that ‘he 
knows everything’, but he should have 
some facility in, and have facilities for, 
finding out.” 

When identifying a find, first of all 
question the group to see what know¬ 
ledge they may have about it, then if 
you can, mention something of interest 

turn to page 75 


Toronto , Canada , February 1964 


49 



THE 

VICE-PRESIDENT'S 

PAGE 


Camping in Alberta, as in most other 
parts of Canada, has been growing 
steadily in recent years. This increased 
interest in camping has caused a great 
search for campsites. We in the Boys’ 
Clubs of Calgary found ourselves in 
this position several years ago. This 
article then, is a sharing of our experi¬ 
ences in the hope that it may be of 
some assistance to camps looking for 
new sites. 

Like many other organizations with 
camping as part of their programme, 
we were looking for a site without the 
outlay of too much capital. Our re¬ 
quirements included such things as 
seclusion, natural facilities (lake and 
wooded area), accessibility, etc. 

Our early approaches to real estate 
groups convinced us that an outright 
purchase of a piece of property was 
out of the question. This we felt be¬ 
cause our modest beginning in camping 
did not warrant the expenditure of 
large sums for property and buildings. 

The next approach taken by our 
Camp Committee was to the Depart¬ 
ment of Lands and Forests. We ex¬ 
plained to them our requirements and 
the approximate area in which we 
wanted to locate, namely the thousands 
of acres of land in the Eastern Rocky 
Mountain Forest Reserve. The depart¬ 
ment was very interested in helping us 
locate a site and proved to be of in¬ 
valuable assistance. 


ON PROCURING 
A CAMPSITE 

by Jack F. Way, 

First Vice President , Alberta, 
Canadian Camping Association, 
Director, Camp Adventure. 


In consultation with the Forestry 
officials, and through the use of maps 
and airphotos, several sites were sug¬ 
gested. It now became a relatively 
straight-forward task of checking and 
evaluating each site. After further con¬ 
sultation, one site was decided upon. 

The site, a small lake in the Foothills, 
did not meet all of our requirements, 
so a temporary free permit was ob¬ 
tained, instead of a long term lease. 
We felt that our “pioneer” type of 
camping with boys could be tried on 
an experimental basis, and if it proved 
to be a workable location, a lease could 
then be taken out. It also gave us a 
chance to become very familiar with the 
entire area and be able to apply for the 
best actual piece of property. This 
latter proved to be true, as our experi¬ 
ences over the next two years showed 
that the area we had originally thought 
suitable, in fact, wasn’t. When after 
some three seasons at the site, our lease 
application was made, there was no 
doubt in our minds as to the best piece 
of land. Our fifteen year lease on the 
20-odd acres will cost 11 s an annual fee 
of ten dollars. The property gives us 
control of over half the lake front and 
hundreds of acres behind the lake, 
making a large piece of land un¬ 
necessary. 

Since then our camp, called Camp 
Adventure, has never looked back. We 
are now in the midst of planning

A HIKING PROGRAMME 


by Dick Caswell, 

Director, Camp Garibaldi, 

New Westminster YMCA-YWCA 


AT CAMP 


Many camps are blessed with lakes 
and waterways which tend to become 
the centre of programme for the camp. 
The camp I direct has a man-made 
pool and mountain stream so water¬ 
front programmes, (swimming, boating, 
canoeing, and sailing) cannot be a major 
emphasis. We have looked for a major 
emphasis and, at one point, found it in 
horseback riding but, due to the in¬ 
creasing cost, were forced to look 
elsewhere. 

Our camp is situated at the base of 
a mountain bordering the Fraser River 
Valley. Most of the campsite is natural 
forest and there is a forest area north 
of the camp which is devoted to forestry 
research by the University of British 
Columbia and to the east is a large 
provincial park. In addition, to the 
ful scenery. Further to the east in 
south and west we have a rural area 
which boasts several pleasant swimming 
and fishing areas. All these were within 
walking distance. Why not emphasize 
hiking? 

At this point, places of interest were 
pinpointed and distances checked. To 
the north we found two lakes (one with 
excellent swimming facilities) and two 
mountain streams for fishing (one also 
had a beautiful secluded swimming 
hole). Maple Ridge Park and David¬ 
son’s Pool was to the south—a wonder¬ 
ful swimming and recreation area which 
could be used for afternoon, all day and 
overnight hikes. 


To the east was Twin Pools on a 
mountain stream which offered good 
swimming and climbing, and Buffalo 
Falls which offered climbing and beauti¬ 
ful scenery. Further to the east, in 
Garibaldi Park, was Mike Lake — a 
pretty mountain basin, the Golden Ears 
—the peak of Mount Blanshard, Alo- 
uette Mountain, Edge Peak and The 
Needle, and beyond that Alouette Lake. 

One problem that now had to be 
faced, was dealing with the elevation of 
each point of interest. We found that 
three miles to Loon Lake was a stiff 
afternoon hike for senior boys, because, 
while they had good trails and roads, 
they had to climb 1100 feet to get there. 
It has been used as a site for all-day 
hikes mainly, and has proven excellent 
because of the swimming and fishing 
facilities. We have found, too, that 
Buffalo Falls is a particularly hazardous 
place and, as a result, has been dropped 
from our list. Since then, we have added 
several points in all directions to our 
hiking programme. We have attempted 
to increase interest in hiking by creat¬ 
ing interest in the natural phenomena— 
water erosion, geological structure, tree 
growth and development, animal tracks 
and habits, and in conservation. 

We have also attempted to scale our 
hiking so that certain sites are con¬ 
sidered to be for the junior campers, 
others for the intermediate and seniors 
and some for the senior boys only. At 
the moment we are considering the 

turn to page 67

Advice from a keen woodsman on the use of . . . 


by C. R. Blackstock 3 
Camp Mazinaw . 


The axe is an ancient hand tool used 
by man to make his way through the 
bush, to protect himself, to build his 
shelter and to clear the land. The axe, 
made famous by Paul Bunyan, is widely 
used throughout the forest industries 
and is coming back into use in many of 
our outdoor recreation pursuits. 

The camp situation is an ideal place 
to teach the use of the axe. Most of 
our campers are from urban centres 
where there is no opportunity and no 
necessity to learn to use it. Any kind 
of tripping is an occasion for the use 
of the axe. The camper should be 
practised in its use before the trip. 

Types of Axes 

There is a great variety in sizes, 
styles of head, and length of handle. 
The hatchet is an axe, perhaps, of a 
very special kind and thus for use in 
special situations. The author prefers 
to have the camper learn the use of a 
two-handed axe first. He learns to 
respect both the better. For camp, the 
27" handle with a head of a pound- 
and-a-quarter to a pound-and-a-half, 
has proved ideal for teaching campers 
of eight years of age and up. They can 
manage the weight without expending 
undue effort. Practice does not become 
tiring. 

The Grip 

The hand gripping the end of the 
shaft or handle remains fixed in 
position. The hand nearer the head 
shifts from near the head at the be¬ 
ginning of the pick-up, to close to the 
other hand when the axe is at the 
shoulder. 


THE AXE 


The Stance 

Holding the axe with both hands 
with the head at the site on the wood 
where the cut is to be made, the feet 
are at right angles to the log, about 18 
to 20 inches away from it. The legs 
should be slightly bent at the knees. 

The Pick-Up 

With the head of the axe on the 
log, the hand nearest the head begins 
the lift as the body is straightened. As 
the axe head is moved to the shoulder 
this hand slides along the handle to a 
position beside the other hand. 

The arms are not completely 
straightened at the elbow. The wrists 
are ready to “cock” the downward 
action. The hands are at about mid¬ 
chest level, the axe is tilted back to 
the side of the shoulder and behind 
the ear. 

The Swing 

Beginning the action in the wrists, 
the head is forced through an arc which 
has as its fixed centre the hands and its 
moving centre the shoulders. As the 
swing nears completion, the shoulders 
and hands are lowered a bit. The pur¬ 
pose is to bring the hands closer to the 
ground than the length of the handle. 
This action prevents the axe head from 
hitting the legs or feet. 

The Bite or Cut 

As the swing is completed the cutting 
edge comes into contact with the wood. 
The angle of the head to the surface 
to be cut is approximately 45° from the 
vertical. The grip of the hands will 


52 


Canadian Camping 



determine this angle. The grip should 
be quite firm once both hands are 
brought together on the handle. 

The position of the head and the 
angle of the handle at the beginning 
of the downward swing affect the angle 
of the head to a lesser extent. 

The Wrist Snap 

As the user becomes more practised 
in the use of the axe, he can be intro¬ 
duced to the wrist snap which comes 
just as the axe hits the wood. To be 
effective, the hands must be close to¬ 
gether for this quick, sharp snap of the 
hands in a downward direction. 

There are many ways in which to 
teach the use of the axe. The action 
is easiest taught when the learner works 
on a log lying on the ground. Once the 
learner can manage and control the axe 
reasonably well in this situation he can 
be taught to drop a tree or stump. 
This requires learning to swing through 
another plane. 

He will probably learn that a 
“bruisin’ ” axe is not much use; that 
the edge on the bit must be keen. He 
should be taught the protective posi¬ 
tions to take in “addressing” the tree 
and to keep the angle of the head to 
the tree at 45° or less to the horizontal. 

Using the axe to split wood requires 
some teaching too. There should always 
be wood between the axe head and 
the axeman. It is well to teach the 
kinds of woods at the same time as the 
learner is acquiring skill in the use of 
the axe. Soft woods — deciduous or 
coniferous—require different treatment 
as does green and dry or dead wood. 

It is important that the learner find 
out that the swing generates the force 
needed to make an effective cut. It 
also lessens the effort put into cutting 
with an axe. There is really no reason 
to wave the axe at full arms’ length 
around behind the shoulders, especially 
during the beginner stage. Controlled, 


directed arm action, with the eye on the 
target gets the best results. 

Once past the beginner stage the 
camper can go on to the many refined 
and special uses of the axe. To do 
this he needs opportunity to practise, 
stimulus to use it constructively and 
motivation to create with it. 

The use of the axe is best taught to 
small groups in a place set aside for 
this purpose. As with any other activity 
there are certain hazards which have 
to be taken into account. Good teach¬ 
ing eliminates most of these. If the 
tool is respected and the user learns to 
manage it he can derive benefit and 
pleasure from using it. 

Let’s have our campers in the bush 
and on the trail take along the axe, 
knowing well how to use, where and 
when to put it to work; and how to 
take care of it. The camper axeman 
will re-echo that great shout which rang 
so commonly through the bush, “Tim¬ 
ber!” He will expose the growth rings 
which reveal the weather and soil 
nutrients of the past. He will discover 
the quality and smell of dry white 
cedar and the tough pitchiness of white 
pine roots. He will learn the stinging 
tingle from the handle as the head goes 
against a dead piece of hardwood. 

In many ways to be an able axeman 
will permit a more detailed exploration 
of the world around him and also more 
comfortable living in the bush and on 
the trail. 

Editor’s Note: While we feel sure 
that a true axeman has a great respect 
for the long process of growth that 
makes a tree and would never wantonly 
chop down valuable timber, it might 
be well for those teaching axemanship 
to advise the learners to practise on 
either dead or fallen wood or on trees 
that should be cut down for some valid 
reason. Here is an opportunity for dis¬ 
cussing the importance of conservation. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, February 1964

Anne Vail 


It was an historic gathering when 
tlie Canadian Camping Association, no 
longer a section of the American Camp¬ 
ing Association, held its first conference 
in Ottawa in May of 1947. We 
gathered as representatives of our pro¬ 
vincial sections in the conference room 
of the Chateau Laurier. There in our 
national capital, our field of vision 
widened as we saw Canadian Camping 
as a nation-wide movement. It was 
there that we elected Miss Anne Vail 
of Montreal to be secretary of the 
C.C.A. under the presidency of Miss 
Dais Gass. 

Anne Vail brought to her position a 
great sense of responsibility and en¬ 
thusiasm, and within a few months had 
planned to visit the newly formed 
Associations of the western provinces. 
It was my privilege to accompany Anne 
on this tour and it was a memorable 
adventure. We met first the camp 
leaders of Vancouver, then those of 
Calgary, Edmonton, Saskatoon and 
Winnipeg. With every group of camp 
leaders Anne was immediately “at 
home.” In her friendly informal man-

A Welcome addition to our series . . . 


WHY I DIRECT A CAMP 


After settling on a ranch nestled in 
a valley surrounded by hills and with 
our own three children off to the cities 
to better paying positions, my husband 
and I felt very lonely without young 
people around. We thought what a 
delightful spot it would be here for 
city children to spend a holiday and 
learn more about the animals and pets 
that we had to share as well as enjoy 
the healthy wide open spaces. So we 
started a children’s ranch camp. 

My husband being an experienced 
horseman was able to play a very im¬ 
portant part in our particular camp. 
We were both westerners, having grown 
up at the foothills of the Rockies in 
B.C. I used to spend two weeks every 
summer at our church camp in the 
Fraser Valley. My Sunday school 
teacher supervised our group. This was 
where I learned to swim, learned to get 
along with a group. The long hikes 
were very interesting and adventurous. 
Best of all I loved night time when we 
were grouped around the camp fire 
discussing many interesting topics and 
sharing our problems with each other 
before bedding down under the stars. 

After a few years experience in camp¬ 
ing I took an interest in leadership, 
never dreaming that someday I would 
have a camp of my own in the East 
and that my Western camping experi¬ 
ence would help me basically in direct¬ 
ing a camp. 

Camping when I was a camper was 
what I would call “Camping in the 
rough or Pioneer camping.” It was 


by Mrs. Wayne Brush, 

Director , Rolling Acres Ranch. 


good camping though, a wonderful 
experience that I have cherished and 
never forgotten. We learned to get 
along, make sacrifices or make do with 
what we had. We learned sharing with 
our fellow camper. 

I believe our camping is more 
modern to-day. Times change over the 
years and our growing generations 
change with the times. Even so, we 
are still working towards a goal in 
helping to guide our youth in the right 
direction to help build sound bodies 
and minds, and coaching our young 
people in how to co-operate and get 
along with their fellow campers. In 
other words, “Do unto others as you 
wish to be done by.” 

Camping can be adventurous, inter¬ 
esting and educational. I feel that all 
children, and especially those living in 
the city, should spend sometime every 
year at camp, so that they may learn 
about the wonders and mysteries of the 
great outdoors, as well as learn to live 
with a group, have the experience of 
doing things together and sharing. 
Children need space and freedom and 
they need to let go after the school 
term has finished. Just where could 
this possibly take place better than in 
a well guided camp? 

Our first year of directing our camp 
finally materialized. It was a small 
camp, about twenty boys and girls. We

A TRIPPING 

FITNESS PROGRAMME 

by ]. H. Ebbs, M.D. and assistants, 
Camp Wapomeo. 

of a sing song accompanied by the eerie 
call of an owl or loon. All these and 
more await the camper who is properly 
prepared for the adventure. 


“Let’s go tripping.” How often that 
phrase is heard at camp! All through 
the winter, campers and stafT alike 
look forward to canoe trips, studying 
maps, and talking with other trippers 
to learn about the prettiest lakes, the 
best fishing and the most challenging 
portages. 

What is the lure of tripping? What 
makes a canoe trip a rewarding and 
memorable experience? Tripping ofTers 
something to every individual because 
it is a combination of many activities. 
In fact, it is a completely new way of 
life for the city bred person. From 
dawn until bedtime, the tripper learns 
to exist comfortably and safely, with¬ 
out the conveniences of home and away 
from the pressures of an organized 
society. 

There are experiences for every one: 
the thrill of the first night spent under 
the stars; the satisfaction of improving 
a trail, of building a campsite; the 
excitement of seeing Northern lights on 
a crisp August evening; and the fun 


What are the skills necessary for 
tripping? Paddling, swimming, cook¬ 
ing, packing and tent pitching arc, 
perhaps, the essential ones. Every 
camper must have some degree of pro¬ 
ficiency in these skills before setting out 
on the trail. But how many are pre¬ 
pared for the five-mile portage while 
carrying a pack or canoe? And how 
many arc able to paddle a ten-mile 
lake against a strong head wind? These 
aspects of the trip require strength and 
endurance, two qualities often neglected 
in the trip preparation. 

It was with these ideas in mind that 
a tripping fitness programme was 
carried out at Camp Wapomeo, Algon¬ 
quin Park, in the summer of 1962. The 
main aim of the programme was 
gradually to build up the campers* 
strength and endurance so that the first 
few days of a trip would not be a strain 
physically. It was hoped that campers 
who were conditioned at the start of 
their trip, would not tire readily, muscle 
soreness would be eliminated, and thus 
the trip would be more enjoyable. The 
programme was planned as a pilot 
study to determine the effectiveness of 


56 


Canadian Camping 



physical conditioning for tripping and 
the efficiency with which a scientific 
study could be carried on in a camp 
situation. 

The Programme: 

The senior girls, aged 14 to 16, were 
chosen as subjects for the programme. 
Sixty-seven girls were tested when they 
first arrived at camp in order to get 
numerical measures of their organic 
endurance, and strength of hand, arm, 
shoulder and leg. Groups of the same 
age were then assigned by cabin into 
control and experimental groups. The 
control group carried on with the regu¬ 
lar camp programme of swimming, 
canoeing, sailing, riding, etc., while the 
.experimental group was given vigorous 
physical conditioning in addition to 
their normal activities. 

Both groups, control and experi¬ 
mental, were tested before and after 
their trips to measure the following: — 

(a) Changes in physical fitness pro¬ 
duced by canoe trips. 

(b) Any advantage for the experi¬ 
mental group over the control 
group. 

Conditioning Programme: 

In the morning after breakfast, the 
experimental group was led in a series 
of five exercises lasting approximately 
ten minutes. These were designed to 
strengthen the hand, arm, shoulder, 
back, abdominal and leg muscles. Toe¬ 
touching with side-bending, sit-ups, 
back extension, chin-ups from a hori¬ 
zontal position and running on the spot 
were the exercises performed. By in¬ 
creasing the rate and number of repe¬ 
titions of each exercise, the girls 
improved their performances and grad¬ 
ually increased their strength, flexibility 
and endurance. 

The second part of the training pro¬ 
gramme was a mock portage set up in 
camp to duplicate many of the con¬ 


ditions found on the trail; uphill and 
downhill grades, flat ground, a series 
of stepping stones, a low beam to stoop 
under and a fallen tree to walk along. 
The girls were taught the proper way to 
flip packs and use a tump line. Once 
a day each camper in the experimental 
group spent ten minutes on the circular 
portage, the aim being to increase the 
number of circuits completed in the 
time limit. With this incentive, every 
girl competed with herself in an attempt 
to break the record she had set the day 
before. This part of the conditioning 
could be called a modified “Circuit 
Training” programme. 

The conditioning programme con¬ 
tinued for about a week until the senior 
trips went out. Both the control and 
the experimental group took five or 
six day-trips of similar length and 
strenuousness. On their return, all the 
campers were retested for measures of 
strength and endurance. 

Attitudes and Interest of Participants: 

The testing programme met with 
enthusiasm among staff and campers. 
They were interested to be given a 
numerical measure of their strength and 
there was much good natured kidding 
about being a weakling or a “Miss 
Atlas”. Many of the girls asked for 
special exercises to help them improve 
performances. The five formal exercises, 
when done in a group, were fun, and 
many who hoped to lose weight or 
slim down felt that these work outs 
would help. After the first day or so, 
they found the exercises easier to do and 
muscle stiffness was soon worked out 
The majority of those in the experi¬ 
mental group said that they felt better 
for having done the exercises. 

Considerations: 

It was felt that the exercises were 
too formal for the camp situation. 

t 


Toronto, Canada, February 1964 


57 



While formal calisthenics allowed the 
testers to control the study, a regular 
camp programme, designed to improve 
strength and endurance, could achieve 
the same results in a more natural way. 
To be effective, the exercise should be 
strenuous. Endurance swimming, canoe 
sprinting and long distance hikes with 
packs would all be good preparation 
for tripping. Since the activities of 
tripping are usually more strenuous 
than normal camp activities, a gradual 
build up of exercise should increase the 
level of physical fitness and reduce the 
fatigue of tripping. 

The trips started after only one week 
in camp, allowing too little time to show 
much difference in the measures of 
tripping fatigue between the experi¬ 
mental and control groups. It was 
hypothesized that the experimental 
group would be less tired at the trip’s 
end because of their better physical 
condition at the start. Although we 
were not able to prove this satistically, 
the experimental group did report that 
the first day portages were easier to 
cross in comparison to previous year’s 
trips. Their morale was high and there 
were few complaints of stiff or sore 
muscles. The camp as a whole became 
aware of the value of pre-trip con¬ 
ditioning. 

The mock portage proved to be an 
excellent training course. The girls 
learned to carry packs properly and 
improved their ability to balance and 
jump from rock to rock with the weight 
of a pack. The packs should be com¬ 
fortable to carry and not so heavy that 
the campers do not enjoy the experi¬ 


ence. Practical training such as this 
is really the best preparation for 
tripping. 

On analysis of the pilot study, the 
following conclusions were reached: 

(a) Canoe tripping does produce 
marked improvement in physical 
fitness as illustrated by the post¬ 
trip measurements for all campers, 
both control and experimental 
groups. Pulse rates were lower 
after the trips, indicating improved 
respiratory fitness. Scores for back 
strength and leg strength also in¬ 
creased from the first test to the 
second. 

(b) The experimental group did not 
have a noticeable or measurable 
advantage over the control group. 
The pre-trip conditioning pro¬ 
gramme was not long enough to 
produce significant differences be¬ 
tween the two groups. However, 
the experimental group did not 
suffer from muscle stiffness on the 
first day of their trips, a fact which 
helped to speed them on their way 
and increase the enjoyment of the 
trips. 

The study led us to conclude that a 
conditioning programme is desirable for 
campers before they go out on lengthy 
canoe trips. A longer training period 
would likely produce greater effects 
than were observed after a short time. 
To be a suitable part of the camp 
programme, the conditioning should be 
an integral part of all camp activities 
related to tripping, so that skill as well 
as fitness could be improved.

THE PINEGREST 
WOODCRAFT PROGRAMME 

by W. E. Yard , 

Y.M.C.A . Camp Pine Crest. 


Do we really lead our campers to a 
thorough and genuine appreciation for 
the out-of-doors? This question has 
cropped up in our Fall Programme 
Evaluation sessions year after year, and 
in October of 1961 it stimulated a 
series of meetings which carried right 
through 1962 and the Spring of *63. 
These were working sessions, aimed at 
developing a comprehensive plan for a 
more effective “Woodcraft” and Nature 
Programme. 

It was agreed that the programme 
known as “Woodcraft” would involve 
a wide variety of skills and a broad 
field of knowledge, so that every part 
of the camp would be affected. Here 
are some of the general areas: 

Building shelters 
Handling the axe and knife 
Knot tying 

“Safety in the woods” 

Conservation 
Canoeing and portaging 
Tent pitching 
Knowledge about weather 
Identification of birds, mammals, 
insects, and reptiles 
Campfire programming 
Building, extinguishing and 
fighting fires 
Map and compass work 
Splicing and lashing 
Wilderness first aid 
Survival swimming 
Hiking, trail blazing and trail 
marking 


Camp cooking 
Identification of stars and 
constellations 

Identification of trees and wildflowers 

There were to be three stages, and in 
each stage a number of woodcraft skills 
and experiences would be listed on a 
’specially prepared card which the 
camper would carry with him. In¬ 
structors would initial the card when 
the camper had accomplished the re¬ 
quired standard for any item. Some 
form of recognition seemed to be 
appropriate, provided that it was mean¬ 
ingful, and closely related to the pro¬ 
gramme itself. After a great deal of 
searching, the following nomenclature 
was adopted: 

OUTDOORSMAN—This was estab¬ 
lished as the preliminary' level. It 
involved an introduction to many of 
the broad areas of the Woodcraft 
Programme. A blue Woodsman’s 
scarf, cut and sewn by enthusiastic 
staff wives, was the award for this 
level. 

WOODSMAN—This involved greater 
knowledge and experience. A “woods¬ 
man” received a Mora knife—a small 
Swedish steel sheath knife ‘with a 
wooden handle on which a distinctive 
emblem was cut and burned. 

SOURDOUGH — Few people, even 
among staff achieved this level. A

MAKING CAMPCRAFT 
PALATABLE 


by Barry G. Lowes. 
Camp Timberlane 


For too long the tradition seemed to 
be that on a trip campers eat anything. 
A camper who made a face at burned 
oatmeal, the ashes, dirt, grass or flies 
in his stew was a “softy”. 

We believe that good tripping means 
living in the bush as comfortably as 
possible with as little as possible. Food 
should be excellent and meals should be 
imaginative. In an effort to improve 
our menus and our cooking skills, we 
tried something new with our staff at 
pre-camp this year. 

Every lunch was a two hour cook-out 
lunch, a full menu of soup, main course 
and dessert. The menus were arranged 
so that all staff had a chance to try 
standard items and new items. 

Since desserts are the things that 
really make any camper’s eyes light up, 
we purchased a dozen reflector ovens 
and experimented with everything from 
brownies, pizza, pudding cakes, layer 
cakes and pies. Every staff member 
tried his hand at baking so that by the 
end of our pre-camp period they were 
able to bake some delicious desserts. 
Watching is one thing, but when you 
actually bake a pie or cake yourself for 
your own lunch, you learn faster and 
more thoroughly. 

Did it work? Did it carry over? We 
found that reflector cooking became a 
highlight of every trip. The accounts 
of cakes, pies and puddings made and 
consumed were recorded and related 


with pride by returning trippers. We 
also found that right in camp, in¬ 
dividual campers or groups were dis¬ 
covering the thrill of baking with a 
reflector oven. Many evening snacks 
were home-made with loving care by 
the campers, from hand-picked berries. 

We had another motive in these daily 
pre-camp cook-outs for staff Coun¬ 
sellors were carefully organized into 
cooking groups of eight. Each day staff 
were shifted about in such a way that 
everyone had a chance to cook with 
everyone else at some meal. We found 
that when new and old staff worked 
and cooked together, they got to know 
one another much faster than in pre¬ 
vious years. 

The staff was enthusiastic about the 
idea. They liked learning how to cook, 
the fun of cooking and the relaxing, 
socializing that accompanied the meals. 

If you decide to try it, remember to: 

1. Allow two hours for the meal. 

2. Plan your menus carefully. 

3. Have equipment and foods ready 
for distribution. 

4. Assign experienced campcraft per¬ 
sons to supervise the groups. 

5. Make sure the meals are a success. 

6. Make sure that the staff pass along 
their newly found knowledge to 
their campers. 

7. Mix your groups up each day. 

We plan to repeat the programme in 

1964. 

—•

WILDERNESS TRIPPING 

by Walter Wright, 

Trip Leader , Camp Wabanaki 


A tripping programme can be a great 
incentive to a fuller enjoyment of out¬ 
door living if it is carried out in a 
manner which will spark the interest 
of the individual. Nature is an 
amazingly beautiful and ever changing 
wonder which can be fully appreciated 
only if the person knows how to exist 
in its complex surroundings. The duty 
and purpose of the tripping programme 
is to instill both an appreciation of and 
respect for this fact in the minds of 
the trippers. 

1 he principal aim of the programme 
is threefold; firstly, the development of 
a sense of fellowship; secondly, an in¬ 
crease in maturity and integrity; 
thirdly, the opportunity to learn out¬ 
door skills and self sufficiency in remote 
areas. 

The first two of these arc accomp¬ 
lished th rough the demands of the trip 


group. The tripper, usually of four¬ 
teen to sixteen years of age, often comes 
from an urban environment which 
revolves around the Saturday night 
dance and a comfortable home. Placed 
in a group of young men, in isolated 
conditions, the youth must strive to get 
along with the others. It is not easy to 
always agree with those seen constantly 
in such close contact. It demands a 
great deal of maturity and self suf¬ 
ficiency to overlook individual differ¬ 
ences in habits and personality. As well 
as getting along with the group, the 
tripper must learn to respect and obey 
the guide, who, as a fully qualified 
member of the party, has the right to 
expect obedience and respect from 
those placed under his care. He is 
responsible for the welfare, even the 
lives of those charged to him and a 
reasonable state ol order must be main- 

* 


/ oronto, Canada, February 1964 


61 




tained. The youth must recognize the 
authority under which he exists and 
abide it at all times. It may be difficult 
to accept this fact at first, but as the 
trip progresses and he realizes just how 
much he has to learn, it comes more 
easily. 

The third aspect of the aim of such 
a wilderness trip is the most obvious 
and natural one. One cannot survive 
for a long time in the wilds without 
suitable preparation and training. Here 
an untrained person can easily starve in 
the midst of plenty, simply because of 
a lack of adequate preparation. The 
unknown, however beautiful, always 
holds a certain amount of fear and 
loneliness. So it is with Nature. How¬ 
ever, the tripper, when he is equipped 
to be familiar with his surroundings 
will develop a deep respect and rev¬ 
erence for Nature. 

Being at home in one’s environment 
is absolutely necessary for complete 
appreciation of it. This is attained by 
taking instructions to thoroughly fa¬ 
miliarize one with the situation. The 
amount of pleasure derived from a 
wilderness trip stretching over a period 
of about ten days is directly propor¬ 
tional to the skills the trainee has 
previously absorbed. Before embarking 
on such a strenuous undertaking as the 
long trip, the candidate must be in 
perfect physical condition and know 
well the essential boating, camping and 
survival routines. The best way to 
attain these prerequisite skills is to have 
both instruction in them and practical 
experience. Each person must be in¬ 
dividually aware of the problems that 
will be facing him and how to cope 
with them, even though depending to 
some degree on the experience of the 
guide. Certainly, the express moment 
of shooting a rapids is not the time at 
which the bowsman should suddenly 
get the desire for independent action 
by doing what he thinks fit, ignoring 
his companions. He must be able to 


appreciate fully the consequences of 
any action. 

A basic knowledge of tracking, sur¬ 
vival cookery with natural sources, first 
aid, mapping and astronomical naviga¬ 
tion, and safety factors are the minimal 
prerequisite skills that must be com¬ 
pletely mastered before embarking 
upon the extended wilderness trip. They 
must be worked up slowly, the best way 
being to start from the basic overnight 
hike and advancing through the over¬ 
night water hike, and the extended 
water and land hike, until finally the 
stage where one is prepared for a trip 
into the complete wilderness is reached. 
Only then is it reasonably safe for all 
concerned. The development of these 
basic skills can provide the incentive 
for programme activities among camp¬ 
ers in the regular camp. 

The most important factor in enjoy¬ 
ing a trip is the desire to go along. This 
is the prime requisite. Without it, the 
trip will not be a success for others in 
the group. One sullen or dissatisfied 
member is enough to ruin the party. 
Each applicant should be carefully 
screened to ensure that he has the re¬ 
quired knowledge, the physical fitness, 
and the proper attitude of mind. A 
wilderness trip is a lot of hard work 
but it brings a person closer to the 
greatness and beauty of Nature, and 
can result in being a glorious experience. 
Fear of the unknown is banished and 
a sense of real achievement takes its 
place. 

Success can be attained only by a 
joint effort on the part of both the 
guide and the tripper. Close personal 
cooperation is essential. The individual 
must have gained in knowledge and 
exhilaration from a trip. Enthusiastic 
trippers are the best publicity this pro¬ 
gramme can possibly have and if this 
is the end result, then the programme 
has attained its goal: to instill in today’s 
young people a deeper appreciation 
and respect for the world around them. 

—•

Sermons 

Mitber 

&t)e §&un 

A dozen little girls dawdled along to 
their own spot at the lake’s edge. Some 
skipped, hopped or ran, but never in 
a direct line. One stopped to pick up 
a small toad and another an ant. A 
third stood gazing out across the lake, 
looking at nothing in particular. These 
were the eight and nine-year-olds on 
their way to worship. Perhaps you 
might feel that this was no mood in 
which to enter into the Presence of 
God. Yet an essential ingredient of 
worship is the ability to wonder, and 
the unhurried, uninterrupted walk to 
the lake was planned with this in mind. 

Worship lasts about ten minutes; 
sometimes there is a story, a poem, 
a hymn — always there is a prayer. 
“Thank you, God, for rain; thank you, 
God, for sunshine; thank you, God, for 
trees.” The children are asked to take 
turns and can add to the litany any¬ 
thing that they wish. It may be a 
thank you for any of the things around 
camp: lakes, flowers, trees—these are 
the usual. One day, though, I was 
startled to hear, “Thank you, God, for 
Klondike Day”. This special day was 
something that the campers really 
wanted and at last the day was here. 
This was her way of saying thank you 
for the lovely day. 

We have also had thank you’s for 
birds, and one summer for two baby 



by Mary Paton, 
Camp Onaivaw. 


raccoons. One memorable morning 
someone saw a beaver swimming not 
far from shore. “It’s a beaver,” came 
the cry from a small camper. There 
was the beaver working hard — the 
first time the campers had ever seen 
one. One day we had paid a visit to 
the beavcrhouse but no beaver had 
been seen until this morning. We 
stopped and watched him swim busily 
by. Another time the dragonflies were 
emerging from the water and coming 
out of their shells. We watched again. 
We were observing one of the miracles 
of this earth. There seems to be so 
little time lor one to sit and wonder, 
to listen and to watch in these days of 
rush, rush, rush. And so we paused, 
and then returned to worshipping God, 
the Creator. 

Of course the wondering must go 
on all day and every day. Camp staff 
has to be trained to appreciate the 
importance of wondering. Sometimes 
scheduled activities must be postponed, 
because I do believe that wonder is a 
necessity if we would worship or take 
our rightful place in the creative work 
of every day.

from page 55 

increased our number of horses on the 
ranch to give adequate riding and in¬ 
struction to our young guests. Im¬ 
mediately I was nick-named and looked 
up to as Mom and my husband as 
Dad. This was the campers’ doing, and 
I must say it gave our ranch that homey 
atmosphere. 

Soon, it seemed camping was in our 
blood to stay, and we were looking 
forward to every camping season when 
our boys and girls would join us again 
at the ranch and bring many friends 
along too. We were always busy and 
our summer family was a happy group. 

We knew each camper individually 
and loved every one of them. They 
came from far and near. I will never 
forget one little Japanese boy who 
hadn’t been in Canada long and spent 
two weeks camping with us. He was 
toasting a marshmallow at his first 
camp fire and when it was well toasted 
he looked up at me, starry eyed and 
said, “What do I do with it now?” 
This was an entirely new experience 
for him in a strange setting. 

My husband and I find camp life, 
and working with .and guiding our 
young campers very rewarding and 
satisfying. On the whole, we find very 
few problem campers,. but rather a 
camper with a problem. To us this 
is a great challenge and an important 
one. We try to understand and guide 
our campers as a group or individually 
if needed. 

Many of our campers are repeats 
and stay with us over the years and 
train as leaders. In our opinion they 
are our best leaders. Here again is our 
reward as we see our senior campers 
developing and being coached into good 
leaders, so needed today. 

I believe a director can do much for 
a child in the building of good char¬ 
acter, making him trustworthy and 


64 


Canadian Camping 





confident if he can work directly with 
him for a season or half season. One 
must get to know the camper to under¬ 
stand him. 

So to sum it all up, this is as near 
the answer as I can reach. We find 
directing our camp is a. very worthwhile 
challenge, a most, gratifying and re¬ 
warding experience. We are never 
through learning. Sometimes we do 
wonder how long can we keep up the 
pace. Though we grow older each 
year, our campers do keep us young at 
heart.

in ever-changing groups for a fun-filled

In 1948 Miss Vail was invited to 
Britain by the National Council of 
Social Service to do an informal survey 
of Youth Work and Recreation. She 
spent eight months in England, Scot¬ 
ian, Wales, France and Holland visiting 
all kinds of social agencies, and rep¬ 
resented Canada at the Conference of 
International Federation of Settlements 
in Paris. 

Supposedly retiring in 1960, Anne 
left Montreal and returned to her 
native village in New Brunswick. There 
she promptly accepted a teaching 
position. Then she became chairman 
of the School Board and president of 
St. Stephen’s Presbyterial of the United 
Church. Not being able to detach her¬ 
self from camping and campers, she 
went off in 1962 to Camp Wilbaken 
on Lake Memphramagog as director 
of counsellor education, where she 
returned again for a month last summer. 

In summing up Anne Vail’s philos¬ 
ophy it might be said: 

“Many are the added joys 
The passing birthdays give, 

So say a Grace and keep alive 
Completely, while you live.”

BE A WEATHERMAN 

by H. G. Hedies. 


Reprinted from The Young Naturalist, 
monthly bulletin for young people of the 
Federation of Ontario Naturalists , with kind 
permission._ 

It is quite easy to make a bottle 
barometer that will work very well if 
kept indoors, where it will not be 
affected by great temperature changes. 
You will need a bottle with a fairly 
large mouth, a balloon and a soda 
straw. 

Cut the balloon and stretch the rub¬ 
ber over the mouth of the bottle. Hold 
the rubber in place with elastic bands 
stretched around the jar. Using glue or 
cellulose tape, fasten the end of the 
soda straw to the middle of the rubber 
stretched over the mouth of the jar. 
Insert a small stick into the other end 
and sharpen it, so that it will serve as 
a pointer. 

Place the barometer as shown, so 
that the pointer marks one point on a 
graduated scale. Note the changes from 
day to day as the pointer moves to a 
higher mark (higher pressure) or to a 
lower one (lower pressure). 

Can you figure out how the baro¬ 
meter works? When air pressure in¬ 
creases (higher pressure) the rubber is 
pushed in by a small amount. This 
motion raises the pointer. If the atmos¬ 
pheric pressure becomes less (lower 
pressure) there will be greater pressure 
in the bottle than outside, and the air 
in the bottle will push up the rubber. 
This motion, in turn, will lower the 
pointer on the graduated scale. 

This barometer will not work accur¬ 
ately outside, because of temperature 
changes. 

—• 



from page 50 

modest but adequate building facilities 
for the 1964 season. 

In viewing our experiences in retro¬ 
spect, we feel that working with the 
Department of Lands and Forests had 
many advantages for us, namely: 

1. We were able to secure adequate 
land at a small annual fee. 

2. We had the interest of the Depart¬ 
ment of Lands and Forests in 
camping and had their valuable 
assistance and guidance. 

3. Commercial encroachments were 
impossible as it is a restricted area. 

4. The area is patrolled by the Forest 
Ranger, which is especially vital 
during off seasons. 

Similar areas, whether they be Forest 
Reserves, Game Preserves, National or 
Provincial Parks are to be found in 
most parts of Canada. A call at the 
local office of the Dominion or Pro¬ 
vincial Forest Services will bring further 
details in your section. Although there 
are building and other restrictions in 
many of these reserves, they still can 
offer ideal campsites. 

— • 


66 


Canadian Camping 


front page 51 

development of an overnight campsite 
on our property because the nearest 
site suitable for overnight use is a little 
far for the 9 and 10 year olds—par¬ 
ticularly the girls (one and one half 
miles with a major hill). The most 
difficult hike we have attempted is the 
climb of the Golden Ears. We have 
succeeded only once. Other attempts 
have met failure because of adverse 
weather. The hike is about 12 miles 
long and goes up more than one mile 
above camp. It has been attempted by 
hiking to a base camp at around 2200 
feet (about 6 miles), climbing the 
remainder of the mountain and return¬ 
ing to the base camp the next day, and 
hiking back to camp the third day. 
From the summit (5596 feet) one is 
king of all he surveys and is truly 
humbled by the beauty and grandeur 
of God’s handiwork. To the north are 
the snow-covered peaks of the Coastal 
Range, to the south is the fertile Fraser 
River Valley, Mount Baker and Bell¬ 
ingham in the U.S.A. To the west is 
Vancouver, and, across the strait, Van¬ 
couver Island. It is easy from this to 
see the magic that such a hike holds 
for a senior camper. 

One concern has always been safety. 
In this regard basically we have fol¬ 
lowed the policy of the “calculated 
risk”. In all our hiking and particu¬ 
larly with the senior boys, we have felt 
that an element of risk is desirable as 
long as it doesn’t endanger the partici¬ 
pants needlessly. With this in mind we 
feel it is within the scope of the pro¬ 
gramme to encourage the seniors to 
climb the Golden Ears. Special climb¬ 
ing techniques are not necessary — 
caution, stamina and good judgment are 
the needs of the climb. One group of 
boys was to climb the Golden Ears this 
summer but it lacked some of the basic 
features that would give it the needed 
level of safety. 


As a result, they spent a day climb¬ 
ing Alouette Mountain which is much 
lower and easier. This proved to be a 
challenge for all and each enjoyed the 
experience which has helped prepare 
them for the harder climb another 
year. 

Future plans for hiking in our area 
include consideration of survival camp¬ 
ing and extended hikes. Just as .many 
camps send out five-day canoe trips, 
the thought is that in our area it might 
be possible to extend our hikes from 
three to five days. There are hundreds 
of miles of trails and old logging roads 
to the north of camp that could present 
fascinating possibilities for senior boys. 
Carrying food for that time presents 
problems even when dried and de¬ 
hydrated foods are carried. It is at this 
point that the concept of survival camp¬ 
ing enters the picture. A great many 
people lose their lives in this area 
because they lose their way only a short 
distance from help and do not know 
what to do with minimum or no sup¬ 
plies. And yet our forests are full of 
food and protection if we know what 
to use and how to use it. Using the 
concept of survival camping, a group 
could go out with minimum equipment 
and literally “live off the land”. As 
they did this they would be taught 
many principles that have long since 
been lost but which may help them 
save a life someday; and they would be 
challenged to do something beyond the 
ordinary — to test themselves to the 
fullest extent. 

This programme has proven to be a 
blessing in disguise. Through necessity 
we have been able to venture into an 
activity which has many fruits as long 
as it is done on a foundation of good 
planning. 

It is an extremely healthful activity. 
But more than this, on our back door 


Toronto, Canada, February 1964 


67 



we have an opportunity to explore an¬ 
other avenue of fun and learning. Our 
area has history all around it—an old 
logging railway, sluice boxes, and 
mines. These are waiting to be ex¬ 
plored and only hiking, leading the 
campers into areas where few humans 
have ever been, can make it a reality. 

This opportunity may be awaiting 
your campers too!

It seems, in retrospect, that there 
were three primary factors which con¬ 
tributed to the success of this pro¬ 
gramme. First, in the person of “Sass” 
Peepre the Woodcraft programme had 
a highly skilled leader with tremendous 
personal enthusiasm. Secondly, the 
period of preparation was thorough, in¬ 
volving many people who would have 
a share in implementing the eventual 
recommendations. Thirdly, every effort 
was made to avoid the superficial and 
irrelevent: skills, knowledge, and appre¬ 
ciations acquired through this exper¬ 
ience were seen as important in the lives 
of every individual concerned. This 
genuine sense of the worthwhile nature 
of the project was shared throughout 
the entire camp community. 

During the six-day pre-camp orien¬ 
tation course for staff, a good deal of 
emphasis was placed upon the teaching 
methods for the woodcraft skills, and 
everybody was encouraged to become 
as well informed as possible in all areas. 
By the end of this course, many of the 
staff were wearing the knife, which 
identified them as having achieved the 
“Woodsman’s” level. During the sum¬ 
mer, several special evening sessions 
were held for staff, in order to clarify 
teaching methods for various phases of 
the programme. 

When the Summer Camp began, an 
old building was moved to a spot in the 
woods. Campers helped to clear the 
area, and to level up the building which 
was decorated with a pair of moose 
horns and dedicated as “Moose Lodge”, 
the headquarters or home base for the 
Woodcraft programme. At the opening 
dedication of this building, every cabin 
group brought something in the line of 
a nature lore discovery, or a project 
related to the advancement of the

woodcraft idea. From this point on, 
everybody was conscious of a new 
major emphasis sharing the spotlight 
with swimming, canoeing, sailing and 
tripping! 

It would be inappropriate to con¬ 
clude this report without mentioning 
the part which the writings of Ernest 
Thompson Seton have played. During 
the past few years we have been able 
to acquire a considerable library of 
Seton’s books. They contain a wealth 
of information and inspiration, and we 
at Pine Crest are anxious to ackowledge 
the role that the works of this Can¬ 
adian artist, writer, and naturalist have 
played in our own Woodcraft pro¬ 
gramme.

Perhaps one of the cutest stories I’ve 
heard in camping circles for a long time 
comes from Camp Breton Dean, Mira, 
Cape Breton Island, and was told to me 
last summer by Camp Director, Flor¬ 
ence Hare. 

On opening night Florence collected 
all cash and valuables from the new 
arrivals, and was busy entering the sum 
of ninety-five cents from one of the 
younger boys into the Tuck Fund book, 
when she asked little Timmy (staff 
dependent), if this was all the money 
he had to put in the bank. Timmy 
informed her that he would be making 
another deposit the next night. “But”, 
said Florence, “You must put all your 
money in now”. “I can’t,” said Timmy, 
“You see I’ll be getting another 10#

Woodcraft and Outdoor Living Bookshelf 


TREASURY OF 

MEMORY-MAKING 

CAMPFIRES 

Allan A. Macfarlan 

Those of us who know Mr. Mac- 
farlan’s earlier books have looked for¬ 
ward to his latest and have not been 
disappointed. An expert in authentic 
Indian lore of the Northwest Coast 
Indians, he brings to programme 
directors how-to-do information, 
legends, campfire and council ring eti¬ 
quette, challenges, plays, costume 
designs and regalia information. The 
Treasury does that which no other 
book has done, to our knowledge: it 
includes girls’ activities and girls’ cos¬ 
tumes in the contents, as well as the 
authentic art of ceremonial face-paint¬ 
ing, description of the dances and 
magic of the Medicine Men, original 
campfire stories, and true totem pole 
designs. Because the format is over¬ 
size, the book will command respect as 
it serves as the most important encycyo- 
paedia on these topics. We recommend 
it for every camp library, not alone for 
its ceremonial procedures, but for the 
wealth of stories and cultural back¬ 
ground all leaders need. G. R. Welch 
Company, Limited, Toronto. $11.95. 

GETTING ACQUAINTED 
WITH MINERALS 

G. L. English and D. E. Jensen 

In every camp across our continent 
lies abundant opportunity to pursue the 
hobby of rock and mineral collecting, a 
hobby that becomes more and more 
absorbing as deeper knowledge is ac¬ 
quired. That knowledge can only be 
gained through books which have been 


written by experts. Getting Acquainted 
with Minerals is worth its price for the 
breadth and simplicity of its presenta¬ 
tion. Easy-to-read tables and indices, 
further enhanced through illustrations, 
help the beginner to identify colour, 
hardness and crystal formation. The 
first few chapters cannot help but stir 
enthusiasm in introducing the hobby, 
in presenting hints on collecting and 
displaying minerals. Most valuable of 
all, perhaps, is the chapter on field 
equipment, specimen preparation and 
storage, and where to discover this 
precious loot, in which interest, once 
roused, never wanes. McGraw-Hill 
Company of Canada, Limited, Toronto. 
$8.85. 

—E. Flynn. 


Do not miss THE DAY CAMP 
PROGRAM BOOK, prepared by The 
National Recreation Association by 
Virginia W. Musselman. It has a great 
contribution to make in its attitude 
towards Nature Lore and Campcraft. 
It is directed to the ordinary run-of- 
the-mill counsellor who has had no 
training as a naturalist, and gives him 
a step by step programme to follow. I 
believe it should be read and digested 
by every cabin counsellor or day camp 
counsellor. If the material were used, 
we would have far more competent 
campers, campers aware of the world 
around them. I cannot recommend it 
too highly. You will find chapters on 
nature and science, firemaking and 
cooking, knots and lashing, shelters, 
the weather, measuring time and dis¬ 
tance, hiking, use of maps and com¬ 
pass, camp emergencies. 

—M. Go van

THESE BOOKS ARE FOR YOU 


Selected by Eanswythe Flynn. 

* Recommended by P. M. Taschereau 


A nature and woodlore programme 
library can be expanded almost ad 
infinitum, but there must be a beginn¬ 
ing- To this end, the following books 
and smaller brochures are suggested, 
some for sale, others obtainable free of 
charge: 

First, and for every camp, Member¬ 
ship in the Federation of Ontario 
Naturalists, which brings to the member 
regular news releases, notices of meet¬ 
ings, conferences and workshops, as well 
as extensive lists of books, with their 
prices, on Astronomy, Birds, Conserva¬ 
tion, Ecology, Field Guides, Fishes, In¬ 
sects, Mammals, Plants, Reptiles, Rocks 
and Minerals, and Weather. $5 per 
year. 

Also ... a subscriptioyi to “F.O.N.’s 
Young Naturalist,” a monthly news¬ 
paper, punched for looseleaf filing and 
filled with nature stories and knowledge 
even the youngest camper can absorb 
through its understandable style. $1 per 
year. Address: Federation of Ontario 
Naturalists, 170 The Donway West, 
Don Mills, Ont. 

“Getting Acquainted with Minerals” 
— reviewed elsewhere in this issue, 
simple in its presentation, understand¬ 
able by the beginner and invaluable to 
the more advanced expert in the field 
of rock and mineral collecting. $8.85 
from G. R. Welch & Co., Toronto. 

Margaret Waring Buck’s series of 
guide books cover completely each 


topic. “In Ponds and Streams” for 
instance, the flowers, ferns, birds, in¬ 
sects, fishes, snails, snakes, toads, turtles, 
and small mammals are related in their 
appearance during each season. Des¬ 
cription is clear, and illustrations have 
been drawn from actual models. Other 
books in the series: “In Woods And 
Fields;” In Yards and Gardens;” “Pets 
from the Pond;” “Small Pets from 
Woods and Fields” $1.95 in paper; 
$3.25 in cloth, from G. R. Welch & Co., 
Toronto. 

“Native Trees of Canada”* —$1.50, 
Queen’s Printer, Toronto or Montreal. 
A popular publication describing the 
occurrence and characteristics of Can¬ 
adian trees with photographs of leaves, 
bark, and fruit for most species; a copy 
of Native Trees of Canada should be 
in every camp library. 

“Forest Flora of Canada”* —$1.50, 
Queen’s Printer, Toronto or Montreal. 
This publication provides a visual guide 
to the more common plants found with¬ 
in the forest. Composed of photographs 
with the description limited to the 
name and range of the species, it is 
designed to be taken into the forest 
and used by making direct comparisons 
between the plants and the illustrations. 

“Weeds of Canada”* —$1.00, Queen’s 
Printer, Toronto or Montreal. Excel¬ 
lently illustrated and descriptive, this 
is a good manual for use in the identi¬ 
fication of common weeds. 


72 


Canadian Camping 




“Reprinted Plates from “Farm 
Weeds” — $1.00, Queen’s Printer, 
Toronto or Montreal. These are 
coloured plates of common weeds with 
the name of the species beneath. They 
are bound by two removable pins that 
allow the illustrations to be easily taken 
out for mounting. 

“Native Wild Plants of Eastern 
Canada ”*—by F. H. Montgomery— 
about $5.00, The Ryerson Press, Tor¬ 
onto. Limitation to herbaceous species 
with the exclusion of trees and shrubs 
which, with ferns, grasses, sedges and 
the many introduced plants to be found 
treated in other works, keeps this book 
within pocket size. Illustration is with 
line drawings and some coloured plates. 

“A guide to Eastern Canadian Mam¬ 
mals” * by Austin Cameron — 50#, 
Queen’s Printer, Ottawa. This well 
illustrated brochure gives the descrip¬ 
tion, habits and distribution of the land 
and marine mammals, known to occur 
in Eastern Canada. 

“Seashores, A Golden Nature Guide”* 
—about $1.35, available at most book¬ 
stores. A guide to animals and plants 
along the beaches with 458 species in 
full colour. 

“Canadian Atlantic Sea Shells by

NATURE ACTIVITIES AND 
NATURE LEADERSHIP 

“Field Book of Nature Activities”* 
by William Hillcourt, A Putnam Series, 
about $4.00, available at most book¬ 
stores. This book covers hundreds of 
specific suggestions for projects—things 
to do and things to make—in the fields 
of nature, birds, mammals, reptiles, fish, 
insects, wild flowers, and trees. It also 
describes the making of nature collec¬ 
tions and taking of Nature photographs. 
The revised edition which contains 
much added material is called Field 
Book of Conservation and Nature 
Activities —about $6.00 at most book¬ 
stores. 

“Natural History for Young Camp¬ 
ers”* by Herbert Groh—25^, available 
from the Nova Scotia Museum of 
Science, Spring Garden Road, Halifax. 
The author of this pamphlet, one of 
Canada’s finest living naturalists, draws 
from his years of experience with 
Y.M.C.A. and youth camps, church 
groups and nature clubs to outline how 
the camp can be more than merely a 
playground for a couple of weeks of 
sport and outing. 

“Conservation and Nature Activities” 
by Canadian Audubon Society—$3.60 
to educationalists, 423 Sherbourne 
Street, Toronto 5, Ontario. A valuable 
help to the nature leader, providing an 
abundance of useful information on 
nature leadership and suggestions of 
things to do in nature. 

“Edible and Poisonous Mushrooms of 
Canada” —by J. Walton Groves. This 
book, illustrated with over 400 photo¬ 
graphs in black and white and in colour 
should prove very helpful in the identi¬ 
fication of these fungi. The Queen’s 
Printer, Toronto. $6.00.

As you satisfy the group’s curiosity,

Children and Nature Study 

As with any camp activity, some 
campers will be interested and others 
not; some will develop a passing, slight 
or intense interest; others may discover 
an interest which later becomes their 
life work. Many will be attracted more 
to the leader who will take the time 
to listen to them than to his subject. 
At any rate, we have to “catch” them, 
and a sincere personal interest in the 
individual is as important as an inter¬ 
esting informal presentation of the 
subject. 

To make a few generalizations, may 
I say that boys of 9 - 13 years generally 
seem to be enthusiastic about all aspects 
of nature: “Let’s go somewhere and 
do something” such as hiking and ex¬ 
ploring collecting rocks and insects, or 
doing small projects and helping 
around the camp museum. Simple pro¬ 
jects such as keeping and feeding cater¬ 
pillars, grasshoppers, or crickets in a 
jar, planting beans behind glass to 
observe their germination and develop¬ 
ment through the week appeal to them, 
and they like games, quizzes and stories. 
You will find them quick to show 
their “catches” to their friends and 
eager to give out any knowledge they 
have acquired concerning them. 

Somehow it is always to the junior 
camps that I, and the other naturalists 
with whom I have worked, look for¬ 
ward the most. Often little is accomp¬ 
lished in the way of finished projects, 
but the young campers’ fresh enthus¬ 
iasm, warm candour and wrapt atten¬ 
tion to our stories do much to make 
our work a delight and seem so 
worthwhile.

Older campers often enjoy service 
projects, such as making a nature trail, 
or assisting as junior leaders. They are 
capable of more serious work on nature 
projects, and take greater pride and 
care in making collections, with a 
greater satisfaction as a result. Live 
trapping of small mammals (released 
after the group has seen them), pioneer 
use of native natural materials, living 
off the land and working for nature 
badges have all been found to interest 
teen-agers at camp. At times these 
activities lead to the discussion of ques¬ 
tions of a deeper philosophic nature 
dealing with the infinity of space 
(“What is behind the stars?”), God, 
evolution, the Bible. 

Some boys appear to enjoy killing 
living things (notably snakes, frogs, 
even squirrels). Many others will take 
an active part in defending living 
creatures from harm, some objecting to 
the idea of killing an insect for a 
collection. One of the responsibilities 
of the naturalist is to instill the right 
spirit of reverence for life, with a dis¬ 
taste for purposeless killing and yet a 
balanced attitude toward the treatment 
of animal life. This may involve show¬ 
ing the place in nature of snakes and 
frogs, and justifying our killing of 
insects for a collection or our right to 
eat animal flesh. 

Girls may show particular interest in 
wildflowers and plants, observing, draw¬ 
ing and collecting them, in rocks and 
minerals (breaking open rocks often 
reveals sparkling, unweathered sur¬ 
faces), in nature art, and — when 
properly introduced — in small sala¬ 
manders, turtles and even snakes and 
mice. 

Suggestions for Camp Leaders 

As you develop knowledge of an 
interesting subject, your enthusiasm in¬ 
creases and you enjoy communicating 

* 


76 


Canadian Camping 




what you have learned to others. Here 
are a few suggestions of nature pursuits 
for cainp leaders: — 

Look over and buy some of the basic 
nature books that are recommended, 
for yourself and for the camp. The 
field of nature covers a wide range of 
subjects. 

Begin a scrap book of good articles 
from newspapers and magazines. Try 
some of these stories at campfire and 
on rainy days. 

Make a tree leaf collection, and a 
good idea is to press them between the 
pages of Native Trees of Canada. Begin 
a camp nature programme with trees— 
they are the dominant life form, the 
most prominent objects of the land¬ 
scape, and they influence the environ¬ 
ment at most campsites. Then proceed 
to other plants. 

Start a terrarium, or pond life 
aquarium in an old gallon pickle jar, 
and when you pass a pond take time 
out to observe its inhabitants. 

Try keeping some live, small native 
animal: a snail, crickets, caterpillars, a 
salamander, snake, turtle or frog. 

On restless or sleepless nights when 
the sky is clear, you as counsellor might 
take your group outside and point out 
to them some of the constellations. The 
Big Dipper, the Pole Star, and the 
Little Dipper should be familiar to 
most of you as a start. You could 
learn some of the Greek myths relating 
to the stars. 

If you are fortunate enough to have 
the space, set up the nucleus of a camp 
museum—then watch it grow! Leaf 
prints, maps and nature projects, and 
magazine cut-outs could adorn the 
walls. An interested counsellor or 
camper may be appointed curator 
Encourage the campers to bring in 
things and to work on nature projects.

Make use of anyone who has special¬ 
ized knowledge in any of the natural 
sciences, or who may have good stories 
to tell of their experiences in nature. 

Nature Study and The Camp’s 
Spiritual Goal 

Baden-Powell in his last message 
says, “Nature study will show you how 
full of beautiful and wonderful things 
God has made this world for you to 
enjoy.” Nature study is an intimate 
part of that camping experience which 
recreates and permeates the entire 
character with wholesome freshness. 
This knowledge of nature is acquired 
for the most part unconsciously and 
incidentally through the intimate con¬ 
tact with nature that camp life affords. 
Occasions of wonder and discovery 
occur again and again during a camp 
period. It is the function of a camp 
nature study program to multiply these 
occasions and to shift wonder higher 
and deeper. Nature study should open 
the campers’ eyes to the delight and 
interest of the world around him, to 
discern things as they really are, and 
to see his place in a wonderful and 
orderly universe. 

St. Thomas Aquinas writes “Since 
God has made things by His wisdom, 
in considering what God has made we 
can gather the divine wisdom as it is

scattered by a kind of communication 
in God’s works.” Sir Isaac Newton who 
discovered the laws of the motions of 
the heavenly bodies has said: “This 
most beautiful system of sun, planets 
and comets could in nowise come into 
existence without the design and 
ownership of a Being at once intelligent 
and powerful. This Being governs all 
things ... we admire Him for His 
perfections, we venerate and worship 
Him for His Lordship.” 

An interest in nature, especially one 
nurtured from youth, can supply the 
attraction, the excitement and the pur¬ 
pose of a truly worthwhile life-long 
recreation.
